source.title: Quadratic Weak-to-Strong Generalization in Random Feature Networks via Random Matrix Theory

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or corruption; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether a student trained on teacher predictions can outperform its teacher, but in a theoretical random-feature regression setting with population-optimal teachers and early-stopped gradient flow, rather than the original fine-tuning setup and PGR measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical error results and a small population-flow simulation. Related-work results attributed to other studies are not included as rows. It does not test auxiliary confidence losses, ensembles, loss variants, distribution shift, or correlated teacher–student errors.
record.test_reason: A theory paper on whether an infinitely wide random-feature student, trained by early-stopped population gradient flow on an optimal finite-width teacher's predictions, beats the teacher. It derives deterministic-equivalent error asymptotics, so it bears mainly on V5 and on the capacity and stopping-time dependence in V3. A small population-flow simulation (Appendix G) directly shows the student beating the teacher (V1). It does not report PGR and does not use pretrained models.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Early stopping lets an infinitely wide random-feature student beat a finite optimal teacher. For pure harmonic targets with teacher capacity above the target degree, the improvement is quadratic and matches the general lower bound. For mixed targets the outcome depends on stopping time and target energy: incompatible modal times can rule out quadratic improvement, and components beyond teacher capacity give at most a constant-factor gain. All results concern deterministic equivalents and transfer to the ReLU model only under an unproven Gaussian universality assumption.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a random-feature teacher optimally fit to true labels and an infinitely wide student trained on teacher predictions by population gradient flow with early stopping. It studies asymptotic population squared error, rather than pretrained-model fine-tuning or Burns et al.'s PGR measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome changes with teacher capacity exponent α, target harmonic degree and coefficients, and stopping-time exponent γ. For mixed targets, the stop must be compared with the energy in degrees above it.
record.problems: The random spherical ReLU results depend on Gaussian universality and deterministic-equivalent accuracy, which the authors leave conditional and identify as open to control. The student is infinitely wide. Simulation samples are small (32 teachers at d=8 and d=16; 8 at d=28), and the reported sample dimensions are limited.
record.rows_left_out: No primary theorem result was omitted. Algebraic derivations, individual harmonic coefficient calculations, and figure-only curve values were not separately cataloged where the paper gives no separate outcome statement or numerical value.

untested.parts: PGR is not reported. No pretrained language models and no fine-tuning. Direct evidence is only the small ReLU population-flow simulation with a degree-two target.
Auxiliary confidence loss, supervisor ensembles and loss variants are not studied. Early stopping is part of the base procedure, not a compared method.
NLP, chess and reward-modelling tasks; finite student size; representation-based predictors of PGR.
Exploitation of what the supervisor cannot check, distribution shift, and correlated weak/strong errors.
No vision or other modality is studied.

missing.what: Remark 4: if the target degree is not in the activation's kernel (opposite parity), the teacher fit is zero and both errors equal one at all times, so there is no WTS. The tanh and sigmoid examples show which target degrees can be learned.
Leading constants: in Prop. 2 the student/teacher ratio tends to 1/2. In Prop. 3 the optimum is (C^2/48) d^-5 at sigma_4^2 t = log 2; numerical minima lie within 0.1% of the bound.
missing.locator: Appendix E, Remark 3, Table 3; Appendix G.3

missing.what: Simulation precision at d=8 and d=16: 95% half-widths of 9% and 3% of the mean at T2; deterministic equivalents 15% and 4% below the means.

record.verdict_notes: Theorem rows were relinked from V1 to V3/V5, because they are theoretical conditions rather than empirical tests of the basic effect; V1 rests on the r12 simulation. The late-stop regime (r6), where the student copies the teacher's residual, resembles imitation of supervisor errors but does not match any V4 failure mode as stated. The student is infinite-width, and the authors only conjecture that results hold for finite students. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: It does not report PGR; it compares population squared errors. It does not test pretrained language models or ordinary fine-tuning.
Auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors, and loss variants are not tested.
The tested task is spherical-harmonic regression with random features. NLP, chess, reward modelling, finite student-size scaling, and representation predictors are not tested.
No distribution-shift test, test of what a weak supervisor can check, or test of gains shrinking when weak and strong models err alike.

The theory concerns deterministic-equivalent population errors in this random-feature setup; transfer to the spherical ReLU random model is conditional on Gaussian universality and deterministic-equivalent accuracy.
No vision or other non-language modality is studied.
